narrative.executive_summary: The scan found no passing checks: all 16 checks failed, 20 requirements are not satisfied and 65 were not assessed. The most severe gap is that the admin console accepts the default admin/admin login, so anyone who knows it can take control. The newest backup is 480 days old, leaving data recovery at serious risk. Two staff accounts, including an administrator, have no multi-factor authentication. Remote server access allows passwords and direct root login. Running software images contain many fixable critical vulnerabilities. The web server still accepts the outdated TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 protocols and its certificate expired on 2025-01-01.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires access control policies and requires credentials to be changed initially. The scan logged in to the admin console with the factory username and password admin/admin and was let in. These defaults are widely known, so anyone who can reach the console could take full administrative control.
remediation: Change the admin console password away from the default immediately.
Confirm that a login attempt with admin/admin is rejected.
Make changing initial credentials a mandatory step for every new system.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require backup management and the keeping of backup copies of data. Only one backup snapshot was found, dated 2025-06-01, which is 480 days old, far older than the maximum age the profile allows. If data were lost or encrypted by an attacker now, everything created since then could not be restored.
remediation: Restart the scheduled backup job and confirm new snapshots are created regularly.
Set up an alert when the newest snapshot exceeds the profile's maximum age.
Test restoring from a fresh snapshot.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules call for multi-factor authentication, especially for administrator accounts. The accounts kari.admin and ola.tech have no second factor, and new accounts are not required to enrol one-time passwords. A single stolen password would be enough to access these accounts.
remediation: Enrol kari.admin and ola.tech in multi-factor authentication.
Turn on the setting that forces new users to enrol OTP.
Rerun the check to confirm no accounts remain without multi-factor authentication.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require authentication strength that matches the importance of the system. The remote administration service (SSH) accepts passwords as well as keys. Passwords can be guessed or stolen, which weakens protection of the server.
remediation: Disable password authentication in the SSH configuration so only publickey is offered.
Make sure keyboard-interactive and none are also not offered.
Confirm all administrators have working keys before the change.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require administration privileges to be individualised and restricted. The server allows direct login as the shared root account (PermitRootLogin is yes), so it is impossible to tell which person made changes and an attacker gains full control in one step.
remediation: Set PermitRootLogin to no in the SSH configuration.
Have administrators log in with personal accounts and elevate privileges only when needed.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires policies on the use of cryptography. The web server accepts the old TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 protocols in addition to TLSv1.2. Older protocols give weaker protection to data in transit.
remediation: Configure the server so the minimum accepted version is TLSv1.2.
Rerun the check to confirm TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 are refused.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require vulnerabilities to be managed, critical ones to be addressed without undue delay, and security patches to be applied within a reasonable time. Of 6 running images scanned, four contain critical vulnerabilities that already have fixes: nginx:1.20 (17), keycloak 26.3 (4), nis2lab-backup (3) and grafana/loki 3.5.1 (2). No risks have been formally accepted, and the operating system under nginx:1.20 is past end of support. Attackers commonly exploit such known flaws.
remediation: Update the affected images to versions where the fixes are included.
Replace nginx:1.20 with an image whose operating system is still supported.
Record a formal risk acceptance for any vulnerability that cannot be fixed yet.
Rerun the scan to confirm no fixable critical vulnerabilities remain.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require a complete, accurate and up-to-date asset inventory. Three running services, backup, legacy-web and logs, are not in the inventory. Assets that are not recorded tend not to be patched, monitored or owned by anyone.
remediation: Add backup, legacy-web and logs to the asset inventory with an owner, or shut down any that are no longer needed.
Compare the inventory with running services regularly.

gaps.why_it_matters: NIS2 requires significant incidents to be reported to the CSIRT in stages, starting with an early warning. The incident response plan does not mention the 24h early warning, the 72h incident notification, the one-month final report or the CSIRT contact. In a real incident staff may miss legal reporting deadlines.
remediation: Update incident-response.md to describe the 24h early warning, 72h incident notification and one-month final report.
Add the CSIRT contact details to the plan.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require users to be blocked after a predefined number of failed log-in attempts. Brute-force protection is switched off on the staff login system, so an attacker can keep guessing passwords without being stopped.
remediation: Enable brute-force protection (bruteForceProtected) on the staff realm.
Review the failure threshold setting so accounts are blocked after repeated failures.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require authentication strength appropriate to the systems protected. No password policy is set, so there is no minimum length, while the profile expects a minimum length of at least 12. Short passwords are easy to guess.
remediation: Configure a password policy in the login system with a minimum length of at least 12.
Ask users with weak passwords to change them.

gaps.why_it_matters: The rules require logs to be kept for a predefined period to support incident handling. Central logs are deleted after 7 days, while the profile expects at least 90 days. Incidents are often discovered late, and the evidence would already be gone.
remediation: Change the log retention period setting from 7 days to at least 90 days.
Make sure the logs are also backed up.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires policies on the use of cryptography. The web server's certificate expired on 2025-01-01. Browsers show warnings, users may learn to ignore them, and encrypted connections cannot be trusted properly.
remediation: Install a new valid certificate on the web server.
Set up monitoring that warns before the certificate reaches the profile's minimum remaining validity.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires policies on the use of cryptography and encryption. The website answers over unencrypted HTTP instead of redirecting to HTTPS, and it does not send the Strict-Transport-Security header. Visitors may therefore use unencrypted connections that can be read or altered.
remediation: Configure the web server to redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Add the Strict-Transport-Security header to HTTPS responses.

gaps.why_it_matters: The law requires incident handling arrangements. The incident response plan was last reviewed on 2023-02-14, 1319 days ago, while the profile expects a review at least every 365 days. An outdated plan may name wrong people, systems or steps.
remediation: Review and update incident-response.md and record the new review date.
Schedule reviews so the plan never exceeds 365 days since last review.

gaps.why_it_matters: Access control policies should limit password guessing. The SSH service allows 10 login attempts per connection, while the profile expects at most 4. More attempts per connection make guessing easier.
remediation: Set MaxAuthTries to 4 or lower in the SSH configuration.
